chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Ubaydah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The testimony of Muslims is valid against all people of the religions (non-Muslims), and the testimony of people of the religions is not valid against Muslims.

key_terms.أَهْلِ الْمِلَلِ: People of the religions (typically referring to non-Muslims, specifically Ahl al-Kitab or others depending on context)
key_terms.شَهَادَةُ: Testimony or witness testimony in a legal context

ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of non-Muslims valid against Muslims in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* articulates the principle of *ta'addud al-shuhud* (asymmetry of testimony), reflecting the Shia juristic view that the religious integrity (*'adalah*) of a Muslim provides a higher evidentiary standard than that of non-Muslims in mixed courts. It underscores the theological distinction between the covenantal status of Muslims and *Ahl al-Millal* (People of the Denominations), a concept rooted in the Quranic verse 'O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives' (4:135), which establishes the universal duty of testimony while implying the qualifier of faith. This ruling is central to classical *fiqh* debates regarding the admissibility of non-Muslim witnesses in Islamic courts, particularly in financial transactions and civil disputes.
